[Introduction to Statistical Learning]{.custom-title}

[Michael Pearce]{.custom-subtitle} [Math 243]{.custom-subtitle} ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Outline ::: {.nonincremental} In this lecture, we will... - Discuss the syllabus - Make introductions - Overview "Statistical Learning" ::: # Syllabus ## Me **Name**: Michael (he/him) **Email**: [michaelpearce@reed.edu](mailto:michaelpearce@reed.edu) **Office**: Library 386 **Office Hours**: M 12-1pm, W 4-5pm, Th 5-6pm, or [by appointment](https://calendar.app.google/EzeziTJacyi6SyAA8) ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Other Information: - Went to St. Olaf College (Minnesota) and University of Washington - Worked as a statistician at Boeing and Deloitte (consulting) - Research: Bayesian methods for social sciences; ranked data analysis (e.g., voting) ::: ## What is 243? This course will: ::: {.nonincremental} - **In a nutshell:** Expand your "toolbox" for analyzing large, modern, and complex data ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Cover important modeling and predictive techniques (e.g., regression, classification, clustering, tree-based methods, neural networks) - Practice each method in `R` using real/simulated data See syllabus for more detailed learning outcomes ::: ## Class Time ::: {.nonincremental} **Lecture:** Mondays and Wednesdays - Complete a reading before each "lecture" from textbook, *An Introduction to Statistical Learning: with Applications in R*, 2nd Edition (2021) by James, Witten, Hastie, and Tibshirani - **Free online! See the syllabus!** ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Lab:** Fridays - Practice course content and/or work on assignments - Mix of pen-and-paper work, coding activities ::: ## Technology You will need access to a laptop for this course. ::: {.nonincremental} - **Bring a laptop to class every day** - **Please let me know ASAP if you do not have access to a personal laptop!** ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} We will regularly use the `R` programming language - All assignments will be completed in `RStudio` - `RStudio` can be downloaded to your computer (see syllabus) or accessed on the Reed `RStudio` Server: [https://rstudio.reed.edu/](https://rstudio.reed.edu/) ::: ## Communication and Resources ::: {.nonincremental} 1. **Moodle** ← Check this often!! - *announcements, assignments, lecture materials* ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 2. **Gradescope** - *submitting assignments* Please email me if you notice any errors/omissions on Moodle/Gradescope!! ::: ## Avenues for Help This course moves at a fairly brisk pace! Expect yourself to be make mistakes, and embrace them! **You belong here, and struggle is part of the learning.** ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} When you find yourself challenged, I encourage you to seek out help via the following avenues: - **Attend office hours.** I especially welcome you to attend my office hours in the first few weeks to introduce yourself. Coding questions are often best answered in person. - **Work with your peers.** Statistics is colloborative and iterative. Form a study group and work with others in labs. - **Invest in the readings and assignments.** Allow yourself time to soak in this rich and complex material. ::: ## Assessments and Grading Criteria Your grade will be determined via the following course components: ::: {.nonincremental} 1) **Attendance and Participation (about 10%)** 2) **Homework (about 50%)** 3) **Midterm Exams (about 20%)** 4) **Final Project (about 20%)** ::: Let's talk through each of these... ## Attendance and Participation The topics covered in this course are challenging! Attendance and participation will contribute greatly to your learning. ::: {.nonincremental} - I expect all students to attend class regularly. - I expect all students to participate in a way that's most comfortable to them (e.g. engage in class discussions/activities, ask questions, attend office hours, etc.). ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} I understand that attendance is not always possible due to a variety of important reasons. - **I won't penalize your grade for 3 absences.** Each absence beyond 3 will incur a very minor penalty. - **I won't penalize absences in exceptional circumstances** (e.g., medical leave, urgent personal matters, etc.) ::: ## Homework ::: {.nonincremental} Formative opportunities to practice course material. - Usually due Fridays on Gradescope at 6pm - I expect 10 homework assignments. **I have high expectations for your homework submissions**: - Answer questions completely and respond in full sentences - Show your work - Include, annotate, and add comments to your code - Be clear and concise ::: ## Unique Homework Policies ::: {.nonincremental} 1. **Initial Deadlines and Extensions** - Every assignment has an initial deadline. - Twice during the term, you may obtain a 48-hour extension by emailing me; no excuse necessary. Requests must be made *prior* to the due date. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 2. **Resubmissions** - Each assignment may be resubmitted twice for full credit. - Resubmissions for HW 1-6 due at time of Midterm 1; for HW 7--10 due at time of Midterm 2 ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 3. **Alternative Grading** - To promote sustained and thorough engagement with course content, each *problem* is graded on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis; no partial credit! ::: ## Midterm Exams ::: {.nonincremental} To encourage holistic learning and synthesis of the course materials, the course will include two midterms: - Wednesday 10/15 (in-class); Friday 10/17 (take-home due by 6pm) - Friday, 12/5 (in-class); Monday, 12/8 (take-home due by 6pm) Please ensure you will be on campus on these dates! ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Notes:** - **Timed tests are stressful!** I will try to write fair, straightforward exams. Plus, tests are just 20% of your grade! - **Why in-person?** To promote substantive review of material and integrity. ::: ## Final Project You'll work in groups of 2-3 students to analyze a significant research question using a real dataset. ::: {.nonincremental} **4 "In-Progress" Assignments:** 1) **Week 5** --- Proposal 2) **Week 10** --- Exploratory Analysis 3) **Week 12** --- Methods 4) **Week 15** --- Report Draft and Peer Review ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Final Deliverables:** 5) **Finals Week** --- In-Class Presentations 6) **Finals Week** --- Technical Report Due More details to come! ::: ## Course Environment ::: {.nonincremental} **Code of Conduct** **I am absolutely committed to fostering a friendly and inclusive classroom environment in which all students have an equal opportunity to learn and succeed.** - I expect all members of this course to make participation a harassment-free experience for everyone. - I expect everyone to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, healthy, and anti-racist community of learners. Please see the syllabus for additional information, and reach out to me if you would like to discuss any of this further. **Names and Pronouns** Everyone deserves to be addressed correctly. You are always welcome to update your preferred name and pronouns. ::: ## Course Environment (cont.) ::: {.nonincremental} **Disability and Accommodations** - If you have a documented disability in need of accommodations, please reach out to Disability & Accessibility Resources (DAR; dar@reed.edu). - If you have accommodations, please feel free to reach out to discuss them! - Please let me know ASAP if the course-design creates disability-related barriers to your participation (regardless of any formal accommodations). **Academic Integrity** - Please work with your peers! - However, **any work you turn in must be your own!** - You may **not use** generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot) unless explicitely stated. - You may search the internet for help, as long as you avoid direct copying of solutions ::: ## Introductions ::: {.nonincremental} In pairs, please take a few minutes to share: - Name and preferred pronouns (if desired) - Class Year and major - Why you're taking this course - An *unusual or unexpected* fact about yourself I will ask you to introduce your partner to the class ::: # What is Stat Learning? ## Example: Loan Default A **bank** wants to model the **probability customers default on a loan** ::: {.nonincremental} Common Considerations: + Customer age + Marital status + Income ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Q:** What other factors might a bank consider? **Q:** How might each factor relate to probability of default? **Q:** What ethical problems might be present? ::: ## The Setting Let: ::: {.nonincremental} - $Y$ be a **"response variable"** (e.g., prob of default) - $X_1, \dots , X_p$ be $p$ **"predictor variables"** (e.g., age, marital status, income) ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Stat Learning:** the study of the relationships between predictors ($X_1, \dots , X_p$) and a response ($Y$) - (Sometimes we study the relationship among *only* predictors) ::: ## Models We usually assume there is a relationship between predictors and response: $$ Y = \underbrace{f(X_1, \dots, X_p)}_{\text{function of predictors}} + \underbrace{\epsilon}_{\text{"error"}} $$ where $\epsilon$ **("epsilon")** is a random **error** (more on this later!) **Example: Linear regression!** $$\text{Default Prob} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{(Age)}+\beta_2\text{(Married)} + \beta_3\text{(Income)} + \epsilon$$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **The goal of stat learning is to estimate $f$**, given data on $X$ and $Y$. - $f$ captures the "relationship" between $X$ and $Y$ ::: ## Types of Statistical Learning It's helpful to distinguish different types of statistical learning. ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} On the next 4 slides, I'll contrast the following 4 pairs of terms: 1. Prediction vs. Inference Tasks 2. Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Methods 3. Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning 4. Regression vs. Classification Problems ::: ## Prediction vs. Inference ::: {.nonincremental} 1) **Prediction** - Goal: Use a model to make predictions for *new* data - Example: Predict probability of default for a new customer ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 2) **Inference** - Goal: Understand relationships among predictors/response - Example: What's the general relationship between age and loan default? - Example: Is marital status an important predictor of loan default? ::: ::: ## Parametric and Non-Parametric Methods ::: {.nonincremental} 1) **Parametric Methods** - Make assumptions about form of $f$ using **parameters** - Example: Linear regression $$f(X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p$$ where $\beta_0,\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p$ are **parameters** ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 2) **Non-Parametric Methods** - **Forgo assumptions** on the shape of $f$ - Examples: Neural networks, "nearest neighbor" algorithms - **Problems:** Require much more data, uninterpretable, not generalizable *(more on this later!)* ::: ::: ## Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning ::: {.nonincremental} 1) **Supervised Learning** - Models with response variable (and predictors!) - Example: Predicting default risk using age ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 2) **Unsupervised Learning** - Models with *no* response variables - Cluster or detect pattern among observations - Example: Create "social groups" among bank customers using age and income (such as "wealthy Millenials", "low-income retirees", etc.) ::: ::: ## Regression vs. Classification Problems ::: {.nonincremental} 1) **Regression Problems** - Models with **quantitative** response variables - Example: Model probability of wildfire by temperature ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 2) **Classification Problems** - Models with **qualitative** response variables or outputs - Example: Predict if there will/won't be a wildfire by temperature ::: ::: # Recap ## Recap ::: {.nonincremental} Today, we... - Reviewed the syllabus - Defined "Statistical Learning" - Contrasted **prediction vs. inference, (non-)parametric methods, (un)supervised learning, and regression vs. classification problems** Next Time: Lab 1! Before then, please: 1) Carefully read syllabus 2) Complete assigned readings 3) Start Homework 1 (short; initial submission due Friday at 6pm) :::

  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
